f: asks about a person (subject or object)
asks about a thing or action
two senses: 'where' about a place, and 'how' before an adjective/adverb

ex: How do I get to the station?

In which city do you live?

f: the preposition goes to the end of the question; the single word 'hvormed' is formal/literary

f: the preposition goes to the end of the question; the single word 'hvorom' is archaic, only in 'hvorom alting er' (be that as it may)

f: subject form only – as object it becomes mig. The g is silent: sounds like ‘yai’.
one person, informal – the normal way to address anyone today, strangers and bosses included (≈ Russian ты). Object form: dig, possessive: din/dit/dine.
he – for a male person. Object: ham, possessive: hans (or sin/sit/sine when it is his own).
she – object: hende, possessive: hendes. Don't mix up with hund (dog)!

ex: Kender du hende? – Ja, hun er min nabo.
Do you know her? – Yes, she is my neighbour.

f: it, standing for an en-word (common gender): bilen → den. Same form as subject and object. Also ‘that one’ and ‘the’ before adjectives: den røde bil.

ex: Hvor er bilen? – Den står udenfor.
Where is the car? – It is outside.
Jeg kan ikke finde nøglen. Har du set den?
I can't find the key. Have you seen it?

f: it, standing for an et-word (neuter): huset → det. Also the general ‘it / that’ with no specific noun: Det regner. Det er godt. Det ved jeg ikke.

ex: Hvor er huset? – Det ligger ved havnen.
Where is the house? – It is by the harbour.
See you tomorrow! (lit. we see each other)

f: you, plural – always written with a capital I, to tell it apart from i (‘in’) (≈ Russian вы to a group). Object: jer, possessive: jeres.

ex: Are you (all) coming to the party?

f: they – object: dem, possessive: deres. Also ‘the / those’ before plural adjectives: de røde biler. With a capital, De = polite ‘you’.
object form of jeg – after verbs and prepositions: ser mig, til mig, med mig. Also the reflexive: jeg vasker mig.
object form of du: ser dig, til dig. Also the reflexive: du vasker dig. Sounds like ‘dai’.
object form of han: ser ham, med ham. Not used reflexively – ‘he washes himself’ is han vasker sig.
object form of hun: ser hende, med hende. The possessive adds -s: hendes.
object form of vi: ser os, hos os. Also the reflexive: vi glæder os (we look forward).

ex: He helped us with the move.
We are looking forward to the holiday.

f: object form of I: ser jer, til jer. Also the reflexive: sæt jer (sit down).
object form of de: ser dem, med dem. Also ‘those’: dem der (those who). With a capital, Dem = polite ‘you’ as object.

ex: Vi bor hos dem i weekenden.
We are staying with them at the weekend.

f: my, before an en-word: min bil, min mor. Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: mit hus (et-word), mine børn (plural).
my, before an et-word: mit hus, mit navn.
my, before a plural noun: mine børn, mine venner.
your (one owner, informal), before an en-word: din bil, din far. Sounds like ‘deen’.
your (one owner), before an et-word: dit hus, dit navn.
your (one owner), before a plural noun: dine børn, dine sko.
his – one form for all nouns: hans bil, hans hus, hans børn. Only about someone other than the subject: Han tager hans bil = he takes another man's car (his own would be sin bil).

ex: Peter er syg, så jeg låner hans cykel.
Peter is ill, so I'm borrowing his bike.

f: her(s) – one form for all nouns: hendes bil, hendes hus, hendes børn. Same rule as hans: her own (when she is the subject) is sin/sit/sine.
its, when the owner is an en-word and not the subject: bilen og dens ejer. If the owner is the subject, use sin/sit/sine.

ex: Jeg kan lide bogen, men dens slutning er trist.
I like the book, but its ending is sad.

f: its, when the owner is an et-word and not the subject: huset og dets have.

ex: Jeg elsker Danmark og dets natur.
I love Denmark and its nature.

f: our(s) – one form for all nouns: vores bil, vores hus, vores børn. (The old written forms vor / vort / vore are rare today.)
your(s) when talking to several people – one form for all nouns: jeres bil, jeres hus, jeres børn.
their(s) – one form for all nouns. Also the reflexive possessive in the plural: de tager deres bil (their own car). With a capital, Deres = polite ‘your’.
3rd-person reflexive, singular and plural: points back to the subject – han vasker sig, de morer sig. Never a subject. Compare han vasker ham = he washes another man.

ex: The children are looking forward to Christmas.

pron.en: his own, her own, its own (en-word)
f: reflexive possessive, en-word owned: the owner is the subject of the sentence. Han tager sin bil = his own car; han tager hans bil = someone else's. Singular owners only – plural uses deres.

ex: Hun tog sin taske og gik.
She took her bag and left.

pron.en: his own, her own, its own (et-word)
f: reflexive possessive, et-word owned: han solgte sit hus (his own house).

pron.en: his own, her own, its own (plural)
f: reflexive possessive, plural owned: hun besøger sine forældre (her own parents).

ex: The dog plays with its puppies.

f: polite ‘you’, always capitalised (≈ Russian Вы). Rare today – to the elderly, royalty, in formal letters and some customer service. Object: Dem, possessive: Deres. Verb forms are the same as with du.
object form of polite De – capitalised to distinguish it from dem (them).

ex: Vi ringer til Dem i morgen.

f: possessive of polite De – capitalised to distinguish it from deres (their). One form for all nouns.
generic ‘one / you / people’: man siger, at … Extremely common in spoken Danish. Object form: en, possessive: ens.

ex: Hvad gør man, når man er syg?
What do you do when you are ill?
Man siger, at han er rig.

f: reciprocal – vi elsker hinanden. One form; no gender or number changes.
emphasises the person: jeg gør det selv (I'll do it myself). Not the grammatical reflexive – that is mig/dig/sig. Also ‘even’: selv børn kan forstå det.
this, before an en-word: denne bog. Spoken Danish prefers den her bog. Et-word: dette, plural: disse.
this, before an et-word: dette hus. Spoken: det her hus. Also ‘this’ standing alone: dette er min bror.
these, before a plural noun: disse sko. Spoken: de her sko.
before an en-word, or alone about people: er der nogen hjemme? In questions and negatives = ‘any(one)’. Et-word: noget, plural: nogle.
before an et-word or a mass noun, or alone: noget brød, noget at drikke. In questions and negatives = ‘any(thing)’.

ex: Vil du have noget at drikke?
Do you want something to drink?

f: some, before a plural noun: nogle venner. Pronounced exactly like nogen; in speech many Danes don't distinguish them.
nobody, or ‘no’ before an en-word or plural: ingen kom, ingen penge. Et-word: intet (formal) / ingenting.
nothing – the everyday form; intet is the formal / written equivalent (intet problem).
everyone, or ‘all’ before a plural: alle børn. Et-word / ‘everything’: alt.
everything, or ‘all’ before an et-word or mass noun: alt arbejde. Plural: alle.

ex: Do you have everything with you?
Alt i alt gik det godt.
All in all it went well.

f: each / every before an en-word: hver dag. Et-word: hvert år. Also hver anden dag = every other day.
each / every before an et-word: hvert år, hvert barn.
both – begge børn, dem begge. ‘Both things’: begge dele.
another / the other, before an en-word: en anden bil, den anden bil. Et-word: andet, plural: andre. Also the ordinal ‘second’.
other / else, before an et-word or alone: et andet hus, noget andet. Blandt andet = among other things.
other(s), plural: andre mennesker, de andre.
same – always with den/det/de or directly before the noun: den samme bil, samme tid.

ex: We live on the same street.
Det er det samme for mig.
It's all the same to me.
